MAJOR: S3 Put enforces `Immutable` only when `Retention > 0`; with `Immutable` alone nothing is checked or applied (no object-lock/versioning assertion), so callers believe objects are immutable while they remain replaceable — fail-open versus EDP-16.

`retentionFor` accepts `RetentionMode="COMPLIANCE"` on Put with no `ComplianceOptIn`, directly contradicting EDP-16's "COMPLIANCE is a one-way door requiring explicit opt-in"; `PutOptions` has no opt-in field, so the irreversible path is reachable implicitly.

Local immutable check is fail-open: if `readMeta` errors (missing/corrupt meta, pre-existing objects) the key is silently replaced; additionally the mutex is released before meta is written, so two concurrent immutable Puts can both pass the check and last-writer wins.

`objpolicy.WithTenant` is documented as "set by the API auth middleware", but no middleware wiring ships in this diff; `Mint` therefore always returns `ErrTenantCtx` in production — the signed-URL boundary is unreachable dead code until a follow-up.

`S3Store.New` probes object-lock *before* `Ensure` creates the bucket, so a freshly created bucket is permanently flagged lock-incapable for Put until an `ApplyLifecycle` re-probe; probe ordering is inverted.
MINOR: `PartialApplyError` always reports `Applied:"retention"` even for legal-hold-only failures where retention was never applied; operators are told the object is locked when it is not.

`ObjectLifecycle` does not capability-check or map a missing object-lock config to `ErrUnsupported`, so callers get raw provider errors while `ApplyLifecycle` fails typed — inconsistent fail-closed contract.
`stat()` maps every `NoSuchKey` to `os.ErrNotExist`, silently changing the error contract for existing Get/Head callers that matched on minio error codes; `NoSuchVersion` is unhandled.
`LocalStore` takes one global mutex for every Put's rename (not just immutable writes), serializing all writes — an avoidable throughput ceiling under concurrency.
`objpolicy` calls `log.Printf` on every denial with no rate limiting or sampling — trivially exploitable for log flooding under scan/attack traffic.
`objreconcile.Scan` materializes the entire `List` result in memory with no pagination or bound; bucket-scale manifests will OOM.
Invalid manifest entries are counted in `Expected` but excluded from `want`, so `Expected` ≠ matched+missing and report consumers must special-case the arithmetic.
`objpolicy.Stats()`/`ResetStats()` are process-global mutable state, not exported to a metrics backend and not tenant-scoped; weak observability for an enterprise boundary.
Local Put rejects `Retention > 0` but silently ignores `RetentionMode` without it, whereas S3 returns `ErrInvalidPolicy` for the same input — inconsistent validation.
NIT: `Schema = "pf.objreconcile/2"` on a brand-new package; start at `/1` or document the lineage.
`TestScanAbortsOnTransientHeadError` keeps an unused fixture and `_ = st` — dead code.
`UnsupportedError.Provider` derived from `fmt.Sprintf("%T", store)` leaks Go type names into API errors; prefer an explicit `Provider()` on adapters.
`cleanPath`'s `/../` checks after `path.Clean` are unreachable (Clean already resolves them) — dead defensive code that implies a threat model it doesn't actually enforce.
`replace productforge/datastore => ../datastore` in committed go.mod is monorepo-typical but unpinned; add a workspace/lock strategy so module builds are reproducible in CI.
`ObjectLifecycle` on S3 fetches bucket versioning on every call (extra round trip per object) — cache or make it optional.
SUMMARY: Shape and standards compliance are good: capability interface instead of a widened base `ObjectStore`, typed fail-closed errors, deterministic sorted JSON report, read-only reconciler, all new shipped logic in Go per the language rule.

Top risks: immutability is unenforced/fail-open on both providers (S3 ignores `Immutable` without retention; local overwrites on meta read failure), COMPLIANCE is reachable without the mandated opt-in, and the signed-URL boundary is unreachable until auth-middleware wiring lands.
Secondary: object-lock probe ordering in `New`, misleading `PartialApplyError` diagnostics, unbounded in-memory reconciliation, and per-denial log flooding.
